name: ConsensusRecSplit
workload: Single-threaded construction of MPHFs over 100 million random string keys (uniform random length 10-50), plotting space overhead (bits/key) against construction throughput for ConsensusRecSplit versus RecSplit, SIMDRecSplit, ShockHash-RS and bipartite ShockHash-RS/-Flat.
claimed_speedup: Against RecSplit (paper Table 1, 100M random string keys, single-threaded): RecSplit l=12,b=2000 reaches 1.613 bits/key at 25,667 ns/key construction. ConsensusRecSplit k=256,eps=0.1 reaches 1.578 bits/key at 248 ns/key, about 103x faster construction at lower space (derived from page data). ConsensusRecSplit k=32768,eps=0.0005 reaches 1.444 bits/key at 30,245 ns/key, roughly the same time RecSplit needs for 1.613 bits/key. The paper's '>350x faster at 1.489 bits/key' is against bipartite ShockHash-RS (the previous most space-efficient approach), not RecSplit. The project README separately states that on 100M keys, with about an hour of construction, it reaches 1.4448 bits/key (lower bound 1.4427) where RecSplit reaches 1.6127 bits/key.
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ 11.2.0, -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel i7-11700, 2.5GHz base clock, 48KiB/512KiB L1/L2 per core, 16MiB L3
tradeoffs: Very slow in absolute terms at maximum space-efficiency settings (~1 hour for 100M keys); needs a large bucket size (e.g. k=32768) for the best trade-off; combines with a separate threshold-based k-perfect hash layer for cache locality, adding implementation complexity; GPL-3.0 + runtime exception licensing.
caveats: The comparison is by the ConsensusRecSplit authors (their MPHF-Experiments framework), single-threaded, on 100M string keys. The headline '>350x' figure is against bipartite ShockHash-RS, not RecSplit. Queries are not faster: 140-217 ns vs RecSplit's 139-156 ns in Table 1. The paper includes only approaches below 1.6 bits/key, so it has no BBHash/CMPH/PTHash comparison. The latest GitHub release (tag 2026-01-04) points at the 2025-06-23 commit.

name: emphf
workload: Single-core construction and lookup of MPHFs over 1 billion random 64-bit keys, comparing emphf (in-memory seq peeling) against CMPH's CHD algorithm (mphf_benchmark table). Separately compared against the 'phf' library in rchikhi/benchmphf's own 1-billion-key test.
claimed_speedup: On mphf_benchmark (PTHash SIGIR'21 Table 5, 1 billion random 64-bit keys, single core, i9-9900K), emphf builds in 374 s at 2.61 bits/key. CMPH's CHD needs 1972 / 5964 / 23746 s for lambda=4/5/6 (2.17/2.07/2.01 bits/key), so emphf builds about 5.3-63x faster (derived from page data). emphf lookups take 199 ns/key vs CHD's 416-419 ns/key, about 2.1x faster (derived from page data), but emphf uses 0.4-0.6 more bits/key. Separately, the rchikhi/benchmphf README reports emphf's HEM variant building a 1-billion-key MPHF in 770 s using 24 GB, vs the 'phf' library's 3900 s and 48 GB, about 5x faster (derived from page data); that page gives no CMPH numbers.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.2.1, -O3, -march=native (mphf_benchmark harness)
hardware: Intel i9-9900K @3.60GHz, 64GB DDR3 RAM @2.66GHz, Linux 5 (64-bit)
tradeoffs: Noticeably slower lookup (199 ns/key) than BBHash or PTHash in the same table; external-memory scan_mmap mode trades speed for lower construction memory; predates BBHash (2017) and PTHash (2021), so it was never tuned against them.
caveats: The benchmark is the PTHash authors' harness, not emphf's own. emphf builds and looks up faster than CMPH's CHD but uses more space (2.61 vs 2.01-2.17 bits/key). On the same table it is slower than BBHash gamma=1 (253 s build, 170 ns lookup) and much slower at lookup than PTHash. emphf's README makes no CMPH-specific claim; it only calls compute_mphf_seq 'the fastest MPHF construction implementation that we know of' (2013). name: LeMonHash
baseline: Prior monotone MPHF implementations: the Grossi-Ottaviano C++ Centroid Hollow Trie, Hollow Trie and Path Decomposed Trie (ot/path_decomposed_tries), plus the Belazzougui et al. Java implementations from Sux4J of the Hollow Trie Distributor, Hollow Trie, ZFast Trie, LCP, LCP 2-step, PaCo, VLLCP and VLPaCo
workload: Rank queries (monotone minimal perfect hashing) over synthetic 64-bit integer datasets (uniform/normal/exponential, 100M keys) and real-world datasets (text, dna, urls, 5gram, fb, osm; 35M-800M keys), measuring query throughput, construction throughput, and bits/key vs prior MMPHF techniques
claimed_speedup: Abstract: on synthetic random integers, 34% less space than the next larger competitor with about 16x faster queries; on real-world data, up to 19x faster queries than the next larger competitor at similar or better space; up to 2x faster construction than the competitor with the next best space usage (typically Hollow Trie variants); LeMonHash-VL (strings) is within 13% of the best competitors' space with up to 3x faster queries than the next larger competitor. Derived from page data (Table A.1): on uniform keys, 2718 vs 179 kQueries/s = 15.2x against the Java (Sux4J) Hollow Trie at 2.98 vs 4.54 bits/key; against the C++ Hollow Trie (351 kq/s, 4.61 bpk) it is 7.7x; on osm, 1338 vs 73 kq/s = 18.3x against the Java HTDist.
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ 11.1.0, -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3 @ 2.3GHz, Ubuntu 20.04, Linux 5.10.0, single-threaded
tradeoffs: GPLv3 is copyleft (no permissive reuse in proprietary code); like all MPHFs it returns arbitrary output for keys outside the original set; monotone MPHFs preserve key order (unlike plain MPHFs), which is a narrower guarantee that costs more space than a non-order-preserving MPHF; needs epsilon tuning for the PGM bucket mapper and depends on the BuRR retrieval structure and PGM-index as building blocks
caveats: The headline 16x and 19x ratios are against Java (Sux4J) implementations, run on OpenJDK 17 with one unmeasured JIT warm-up run. Against the fastest C++ competitor at similar space, the gap is about 7-8x (derived from Table A.1). The comparison covers only academic MMPHF implementations, not BBHash, CMPH, PTHash, std::map or a sorted-array binary search. An MMPHF preserves key order (it returns the key's rank), so it is a different problem from a plain MPHF. The integer variant supports integer keys only; LeMonHash-VL covers strings. The Path Decomposed Trie crashes on integer inputs. Each experiment ran only twice and was averaged (the paper says variation is small).

name: PHast / PHast+ (bsuccinct-rs "ph" crate)
workload: MPHF-Experiments framework: MPHF construction (1 and 12 threads) and queries on 5*10^7 and 5*10^8 random string keys, each of uniformly random length 10-50 bytes (Tables 5.2/5.3 of arXiv:2504.17918). Uniformly random 64-bit integer keys were used only for parameter tuning (Sec. 5.1) and the ablation study (Sec. 5.4). Measures bits/key, query ns/query, and construction ns/key.
claimed_speedup: At 5*10^7 keys: PHast (S=8, lambda=4.3, EF) reaches 1.94 bit/key, 10 ns/key query, 606 ns/key single-thread construction (69 ns/key at 12 threads), vs PTHash (lambda=5.0, EF) at 2.11 bit/key, 54 ns/key query, 577 ns/key construction (231 ns/key at 12 threads); PHast+ cuts single-thread construction to 61-140 ns/key (an order of magnitude faster than PHast) for 10-15 ns/key query (derived from page data, Table 5.2 of arXiv:2504.17918)
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.84.1 and gcc 12.2.0, both with third-level (-O3-equivalent) and CPU-native optimizations enabled
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5600G @ 3.9 GHz, 6 cores / 12 threads, 384KB/3MB/16MB L1/L2/L3 cache
tradeoffs: PHast/PHast+ trade small space overhead (~1.8-2.3 bits/key) for very simple, fast bucket-placement queries; PHast+ construction is 5-9x faster than PHast single-threaded and parallelizes near-linearly; PtrHash overtakes PHast on very large key sets once evaluation becomes memory-bandwidth bound. The same crate also ships FMPH/FMPHGO, fingerprinting-based MPHFs designed as a faster/smaller alternative to BBHash.
caveats: First-party paper by the PHast authors (Beling, Sanders); the ph crate author is the first author. At 5*10^7 keys, single-thread PHast construction (606 ns/key for S=8, lambda=4.3, EF) is slightly slower than PTHash (577 ns/key). PHast wins on query time (10 vs 54 ns), space (1.94 vs 2.11 bits/key), and 12-thread construction (69 vs 231 ns/key). PtrHash is close on queries, and at 5*10^8 keys it catches up with and may overtake PHast+ (3.2). The comparison is only against other MPHFs (PTHash, PTHash-HEM, PHOBIC, PtrHash, SIMDRecSplit, SicHash, FMPH, FMPHGO, FiPS, Bipartite ShockHash). It does not compare against std::unordered_map or CMPH. The paper left BBHash out of its tests because FMPH is its improved counterpart. GitHub's license detector reports only Apache-2.0, but the README and ph/Cargo.toml state the dual license 'MIT OR Apache-2.0'.

name: PTHash
workload: Construction and lookup of MPHFs over 1 billion uniformly random 64-bit integer keys, single core (construction and lookup single-threaded; BBHash also run with one thread), reproducing Table 5 of the PTHash SIGIR'21 paper.
claimed_speedup: At similar space (~3 bits/key) on 1 billion random 64-bit keys, single core, PTHash lookups take 37 ns/key (C-C, alpha=0.99, c=7, 3.23 bits/key) and 55 ns/key (D-D, alpha=0.94, c=7, 2.99 bits/key), vs 170 ns/key for BBHash gamma=1 (3.06 bits/key). That is about 3.1-4.6x faster lookups (derived from page data); the paper text says 3-4.5x vs BBHash gamma=1,2. BBHash builds faster at that setting (253 s vs 689-1042 s for these PTHash variants).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.2.1, -O3 -march=native (PTHash SIGIR'21 paper Sec. 5; mphf_benchmark CMakeLists.txt sets -O3 -march=native)
hardware: Intel i9-9900K @3.60GHz, 64GB DDR3 RAM @2.66GHz, Linux 5 (64-bit)
tradeoffs: Offline/batch construction only (not incremental); needs a 64-bit-bucket-id compile flag beyond 2^32 buckets; several encoder/bucketer configs (lambda, alpha, dense vs partitioned) must be tuned for the desired space/time trade-off.
caveats: The benchmark is by the PTHash authors, and the README table reproduces their own SIGIR'21 Table 5. That table includes GOV, which is Java-only and cannot be run by the harness. name: RecSplit (Sux C++ library)
workload: Construction and lookup of MPHFs over 1 billion random 64-bit keys, single machine, comparing RecSplit against CMPH's CHD algorithm (table reproducing Table 5 of the PTHash SIGIR'21 paper).
claimed_speedup: On 1 billion random 64-bit keys, RecSplit (l=8, b=100) builds in 936 s at 1.80 bits/key with 204 ns/key lookup. CMPH's CHD takes 1972 s (lambda=4, 2.17 bits/key, 419 ns), 5964 s (lambda=5, 2.07 bits/key, 417 ns) and 23746 s (lambda=6, 2.01 bits/key, 416 ns). That makes CHD about 2.1-25x slower to build and about 2x slower to query, while using more space (derived from page data). RecSplit (l=5, b=5) builds in 233 s at 2.95 bits/key, about 8.5x faster than CHD lambda=4 (derived from page data). BBHash builds faster (100-253 s) but needs 3.06-6.87 bits/key.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.2.1, -O3, -march=native (mphf_benchmark harness, same environment as the PTHash paper)
hardware: Intel i9-9900K @3.60GHz, 64GB DDR3 RAM @2.66GHz, Linux 5 (64-bit)
tradeoffs: Recursive-splitting construction has higher constant factors than fingerprinting approaches (BBHash) at very low target space; single-header C++ template library requires manual integration; licensed GPL-3.0 + GCC Runtime Library Exception.

Queries are slightly slower (114-118 ns vs 97 ns).

hardware: Intel i7-11700, 8 cores, 2.5GHz base, Ubuntu 22.04

name: SimdRecSplit / GpuRecSplit
workload: Single-threaded MPHF construction for 10 million keys, which are random strings of uniform length 10-50 (not 64-bit integers). SIMDRecSplit is compared against BBHash, RecSplit, PTHash and SicHash on bits/key and construction/query ns per key (paper Table 3). The GPU and multi-core speedups come from paper Table 1 (5 million objects, random 128-bit master hash codes, relative to the original single-threaded RecSplit).
claimed_speedup: Single-threaded on 10M keys, SIMDRecSplit (l=5, b=5) builds in 49 ns/key at 2.96 bits/key. BBHash gamma=1.0 needs 208 ns/key at 3.059 bits/key, so SIMDRecSplit is about 4.2x faster and smaller (derived from page data). BBHash gamma=5.0 is about as fast (50 ns/key) but needs 6.871 bits/key. Against the original RecSplit, speedups reach 50x single-threaded SIMD, 239x with 16 threads and 5438x on an RTX 3090 GPU (l=18, b=50, 5M objects; paper Table 1).
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ (gcc) 11.2.0, -O3 -march=native; CUDA 11 for the GPU variant
hardware: Intel i7-11700 (8 cores/16 threads, 2.5GHz base, AVX-512); NVIDIA RTX 3090 for the GPU variant
tradeoffs: GPU variant requires CUDA hardware/drivers; SIMD variant needs AVX support (falls back to slower emulated SIMD without it); licensed GPL-3.0 + GCC Runtime Library Exception (same terms as libstdc++), which is more restrictive than BBHash's/PTHash's permissive licenses.
caveats: The BBHash numbers were checked by hand against the Table 3 PDF (v2, 5 Jul 2023) and match. Table 3 runs BBHash single-threaded. BBHash is a parallel code, but Figure 6 shows it scales poorly, so this does not flip the result. SIMDRecSplit queries are slower than BBHash (71 vs 51 ns/key at the compared settings). The README's headline table compares only against RecSplit. The SIMD path targets x86 AVX-512/AVX2, and the GPU path needs CUDA.

name: LPHash
workload: An MPHF over the distinct k-mers of 5 whole-genome datasets, from Yeast (11.6M k-mers) to Human (2.77G k-mers), given as spectrum-preserving string sets (BCALM2 + UST stitched unitigs), for k=31..63. Space is measured in bits/k-mer. Queries are about 100M k-mers from human chr13, measured in streaming and random order on a single core.
claimed_speedup: Paper Table 3: partitioned LPHash at k=63 uses 0.53, 0.64, 0.83, 0.58 and 0.87 bits/k-mer on Yeast, Elegans, Cod, Kestrel and Human. BBHash-v1 uses 3.71 bits/k-mer, BBHash-v2 3.06, PTHash-v1 2.58-2.76 and PTHash-v2 2.04-2.20. The paper states LPHash is 5.1x, 4.1x, 3.2x, 4.4x and 3x smaller than PTHash-v1 and 2.3-3.7x smaller than PTHash-v2. Against BBHash-v2 it is about 3.5-5.8x smaller (derived from page data). At k=31, LPHash uses 1.18-1.74 bits/k-mer. For streaming queries the paper says: 'Compared to BBHash, LPHash is 2x faster on Yeast and up to 4-5x faster on the larger datasets.' The README's claim of '< 0.9 bits/k-mer vs 1.44 lower bound and 2-3 bits/k-mer for practical constructions' matches these tables.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 11.2.0, -O3 -march=native (paper). The repo CMakeLists.txt also adds -std=c++17 -mbmi2 -msse4.2.
hardware: Intel i9-9900K @ 3.60 GHz, 64 GB RAM, Linux 5.13.0. Queries ran on 1 core. Builds used 4 threads.
tradeoffs: Specialized for consecutive/overlapping k-mer key sets in bioinformatics, not a general-purpose MPHF; requires k-mer-specific preprocessing (stitched unitig files); partitioned vs. unpartitioned construction is a further trade-off between memory and speed.
caveats: The space win applies only to overlapping k-mers from spectrum-preserving string sets. The paper stresses that BBHash and PTHash are general-purpose MPHFs for arbitrary keys. Random-order (non-streaming) queries are slower than PTHash. Construction is slower than BBHash-v1: Table 5 gives 05:30 vs 00:48 on Cod and 07:25 vs 04:13 on Human. Datasets are on Zenodo (record 7239205). The last commit on the default branch (main) is 2023-07-19. The dev branch has a later commit, dated 2023-11-18.

name: MorphisHash
workload: (1) A single Bipartite MorphisHash vs Bipartite ShockHash base case (n up to about 64 keys): idealized space overhead and average successful seed (Figs. 2-3). (2) Partitioned MorphisHash-RS/-Flat vs Bipartite ShockHash-RS/-Flat (and CONSENSUS-RS, PHOBIC) on 100 million keys in the MPHF-Experiments framework: space (bits/key), query time (ns/query) and construction time (ns/key) (Table 1, Fig. 5).
claimed_speedup: Abstract: MorphisHash saves Theta(ln n) bits in expectation vs ShockHash, 'a factor of 20 less space overhead in practice'. That factor is for a single unpartitioned base case (Sec. 6.1, Bipartite MorphisHash with b=n-6): under 0.1 bits of total overhead vs about 2 bits for Bipartite ShockHash, at the cost of about 4x more seed tests. For a full MPHF on 100M keys (Table 1), Bip. MorphisHash-RS (n=52, b=n-4) gives 1.501 bits/key, 137 ns/query and 6,669 ns/key construction. Bip. ShockHash-RS (n=66) gives 1.523 bits/key, 147 ns/query and 7,186 ns/key. This is about 0.02 bits/key, or 27% less overhead, at equal construction time. At an equal 1.489 bits/key, MorphisHash-RS builds in 8,085 ns/key vs 172,738 ns/key for ShockHash-RS, which the paper calls about 21x faster construction.
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700 (48 KiB L1d and 512 KiB L2 per core, 16 MiB L3), 64 GiB dual-channel DDR4-3200
tradeoffs: GitHub fork of ByteHamster/ShockHash that changes the seed-encoding scheme to remove redundant key-to-position mappings, reducing space at the same query complexity; integrated as its own contender in ByteHamster/MPHF-Experiments; very low external adoption (3 stars) despite the algorithmic improvement
caveats: The '20x less space overhead' figure applies to the per-base-case redundancy of ShockHash, not to total bits/key. For full 100M-key MPHFs, the gain is about 0.01-0.02 bits/key at equal construction time, or about 21x faster construction at equal space (1.489 bits/key). The paper does not state the compiler or flags; the MorphisHash and MPHF-Experiments CMake files default to a Release build with -march=native. The baseline (ShockHash) is an advanced research MPHF by the same group, not std::unordered_map, CMPH or BBHash. Single-author paper that uses the group's own benchmark framework. The repo is a GitHub fork of ByteHamster/ShockHash with 3 stars. The newest commit on any branch is 2025-07-03 (the pushed_at of 2025-11-13 adds no newer commit).

name: PHOBIC-GPU
workload: MPHF construction on 100 million random string keys (random length 10-50 characters). GPU construction (plus 8 CPU threads) is compared with CPU PHOBIC at 1 and 8 threads, for the same configurations (lambda=9, 13, 14; interleaved Rice/Compact coding). All queries run on the CPU.
claimed_speedup: PHOBIC-GPU constructs an MPHF at 2.17 bits/key in 28 ns/key (GPU + 8 CPU threads), and the MPHF answers queries in 37 ns on the CPU (abstract, Table 1). At lambda=9.0 with interleaved Rice coding, PHOBIC-GPU gives 1.76 bits/key, 52 ns/query and 27 ns/key construction. CPU PHOBIC gives 1.74 bits/key, 50 ns/query, 9,171 ns/key (1 thread) and 1,781 ns/key (8 threads). The paper states a 62x construction speedup over the multithreaded CPU implementation and about 30x lower energy (Table 1, Sec. 5.2 of arXiv:2404.18497).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.4.0, -march=native -O3; GPU accessed via Vulkan 1.3.236
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700 (48 KiB L1d and 512 KiB L2 per core), 64 GiB DDR4, Ubuntu 22.04.1; GPU: Nvidia RTX 3090
tradeoffs: Requires Vulkan-capable GPU for construction; only construction is GPU-accelerated, queries still run on CPU; the CPU PHOBIC implementation it accelerates lives inside the already-catalogued jermp/pthash repo (branch 'phobic'), so this repo only supplies the GPU construction path
caveats: The speedup compares an RTX 3090 GPU with an 8-thread i7-11700 CPU, so it depends on the hardware. The paper notes the GPU only wins for large n and large lambda; at small lambda, transferring the input to the GPU dominates. Queries are not faster: they run on the CPU and are the same as CPU PHOBIC. The system draws about 405 W during the GPU search vs 195 W for the multithreaded CPU. Needs a Vulkan-capable GPU. The baseline is the authors' own CPU PHOBIC (jermp/pthash phobic branch), not std::unordered_map, CMPH or BBHash. Only 4 GitHub stars, and the last commit was 2025-07-03.

name: PtrHash
baseline: BBHash and CMPH (CHD) in the arXiv 2506.06536 survey; PTHash and PHOBIC (plus CMPH CHD) in the SEA 2025 paper arXiv 2502.15539
workload: Survey Table 6: 100M random strings of length 10-50, single-threaded construction, then 100M queries, via MPHF-Experiments tableSurvey. SEA 2025 paper Table 2: 300M random strings of length 10-50 via MPHF-Experiments, 6-thread construction where supported. SEA 2025 paper Table 1: 1e9 random 64-bit integer keys hashed with FxHash, for-loop and prefetched streaming queries.
claimed_speedup: Survey arXiv 2506.06536v3, Table 6 (100M random string keys, single-threaded). PtrHash with lambda=3.0, linear, vec uses 2.990 bits/key, queries in 45 ns and builds in 141 ns/key. PtrHash with lambda=4.0, cubic, EF uses 2.118 bits/key, queries in 47 ns and builds in 358 ns/key. BBHash gamma=5.0 (6.870 bits/key) queries in 127 ns and builds in 157 ns/key. BBHash gamma=1.5 (3.293 bits/key) queries in 173 ns and builds in 273 ns/key. CMPH CHD lambda=4 (2.166 bits/key) queries in 356 ns and builds in 1,522 ns/key. PtrHash queries are about 2.7x-3.8x faster than BBHash and 7.6x-7.9x faster than CHD. Fast PtrHash builds 1.1x-1.9x faster than BBHash, and CHD builds 4.3x-10.8x slower than PtrHash (derived from page data). SEA 2025 paper arXiv 2502.15539v2, Table 2 (300M string keys, 6 threads): default PtrHash (2.40 bits/key) queries in 37 ns and 23 ns streaming. The fastest PTHash config (C-C) takes 77 ns, which gives the paper's stated 2.1x and 3.3x. CMPH CHD takes 542 ns, about 14.6x slower than default PtrHash (derived from page data). Paper Table 1 (1e9 integer keys): the MPHF for-loop query takes 12.5-14.2 ns only with the fast parameters (2.76-3.00 bits/key). It takes 20.0-21.7 ns with the default or compact parameters (2.09-2.62 bits/key). Streaming takes 8.6-9.7 ns in all configurations, and 8.6-8.8 ns with the Vec or CacheLineEF remap.
compiler_and_flags: Survey: GNU C++ 14.2.0 with -O3 -march=native (CMake Release), and Rust 1.85.0 in release mode with target-cpu=native. PtrHash is linked from the ptr_hash crate pinned at =1.1.0 through a Rust staticlib FFI contender. SEA paper: no compiler version is stated. The PtrHash repo builds with -C target-cpu=native (.cargo/config.toml on master) and a release profile with lto=thin.
hardware: Survey: Intel Core i7-11700 (8 cores, 16 threads), pinned to its 2.5 GHz base clock, Rocky Linux 9.5, Linux 5.14.0. SEA paper: Intel Core i7-10750H, 6 cores, hyper-threading disabled, frequency pinned to 2.6 GHz, 64 GiB DDR4-3200.
tradeoffs: Rust implementation; an unofficial, ambiguously-licensed C++ port exists (bassiounix/PtrHash-cc, made for an LLVM libc RFC) but has no independent benchmarks; CompactPtrHash trades ~2x slower construction for smaller size; needs sharding for keys that don't fit in RAM
caveats: PtrHash is a Rust crate with no C/C++ API. C++ use needs FFI, as MPHF-Experiments does. Neither source compares against std::unordered_map. The survey measured ptr_hash 1.1.0, and the current crate is 2.1.1. In survey Table 6, PHast and PHast+ (Rust) query slightly faster than PtrHash (38-44 ns vs 45-47 ns) at about 1.85-2.07 bits/key, so PtrHash is not the fastest-query MPHF there. Compact PtrHash builds slower than BBHash gamma=1.5 single-threaded (358 vs 273 ns/key). The paper's 2.1x and 3.3x are measured against the fastest PTHash configuration. Its 12 ns / 8 ns integer-key figures skip string hashing, and the 12 ns for-loop needs about 3 bits/key. The README large-input table was run at 3.6 GHz, not the paper's pinned 2.6 GHz. The previous caveat was wrong: the paper never says BBHash/CMPH-style methods are omitted as not competitive. SEA Table 2 includes CMPH's CHD and the fingerprinting methods FMPH, FMPHGO and FiPS. The survey is an arXiv preprint (v3, 2026-02-05) with no journal reference.

name: Sphinx
baseline: DHT (Delta Hash Table, a dynamic perfect hash table) / RSQF / Aleph Filter / Adaptive Aleph Filter (state-of-the-art fingerprint and perfect-hash indexes for log-structured hash tables / key-value stores)
workload: Average and tail-99 query/update/insertion latency and memory footprint (bits/entry) of an in-memory, Optane, and SSD-resident LSH-table index over up to 10^8 keys, against DHT, DHT-expandable, RSQF, Aleph Filter and Adaptive Aleph Filter C++ implementations
claimed_speedup: Abstract: about 2x lower query latency, update latency and memory footprint than the best alternatives. Fig. 6: zero false positives for queries to existing keys, and at most half the memory of the other baselines. In memory (Fig. 8), Sphinx has the lowest average and p99 query/update latency. Its average insertion is slightly slower than some baselines (read-before-write); Sphinx-4 (4 reserve bits) beats all baselines on every in-memory metric. On Optane, Sphinx variants are fastest. On SSD (Fig. 9), they match or beat all baselines, with only a slight gap to DHT-expandable under a uniform workload. Under skew at 90-99% cache hit rate, Sphinx is 10-35% faster than DHT-expandable (Fig. 10A).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.4.0 (benchmark/reproducibility.md, 'version installed or later'); -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native -mbmi2 (CMakeLists.txt). CMakeLists.txt also sets an RPATH to /usr/local/gcc-14.1.0 and has a commented-out GCC 14.1.0 compiler path.
hardware: Platform 1: Intel Xeon W7-2495X (24 cores/48 threads, 2.5GHz), 1.9MB L1/48MB L2/45MB L3, 512GB NVMe SSD (OS) + 2TB Samsung 980 Pro SSD (benchmark drive), Ubuntu 22.04; Platform 2: dual Intel Xeon Silver 4314 (32 cores/64 threads, 2.4GHz) with 256GB RAM + 496GB Intel Optane Persistent Memory 200 Series, Ubuntu 22.04
stars_or_usage: 22 stars; PVLDB vol. 18(11), pp. 4424-4437 (2025); the paper's PVLDB Artifact Availability section points to the repo
tradeoffs: Designed specifically as an in-memory index for LSH-table / log-structured key-value stores (not a general-purpose associative container); relies on x86 rank/select instructions (POPCNT, PEXT, TZCNT) for full speed; static succinct trie-based decoder is built for a fixed key set per block and expands via block-group splitting rather than arbitrary rehashing; DHT baseline was the authors' own C++ re-implementation since the original DHT code is closed-source
caveats: The baselines are LSH-table indexes and filters (DHT, RSQF, Aleph Filter), not std::unordered_map or MPHFs such as BBHash, CMPH or PTHash. DHT is the authors' own C++ reimplementation, because the original is closed-source. RSQF and Aleph Filter come from the Memento Filter codebase. Sphinx is a dynamic succinct perfect hash table (a key-to-payload index), not a static MPHF. It is x86-only and needs BMI2 PDEP/PEXT. The 2x headline comes from the abstract; the figures carry the per-experiment detail and there is no numeric table. The compiler version comes from the repo's reproducibility doc, not the paper, and the CMake RPATH points to GCC 14.1.0, so the exact compiler for the paper runs is not certain.

workload: Google Benchmark loop (benchmark.cpp) looks up every identifier token in three corpora. map-to-tokens.cpp builds the corpora from jquery-3.5.1.js: keywords-only, non-keywords-only, and mixed, whitespace-padded to ~287 KB each. Lookups run against the JavaScript keyword set (token.gperf). Each implementation is compiled as a shared library and loaded with dlopen: dozens of generated pht variants, gperf 3.1 option combos, mygperf, bsearch and linear scans, frozen::unordered_map, std::unordered_map, and Rust phf and std::collections::HashMap.
claimed_speedup: notes.txt (author's dev log, approximate '~' figures): on the nonkeywords corpus, pht with the icrc32 hasher and --string-compare=check1memcmp (~69 us) beats gperf default (~95 us) [~1.38x, derived from page data]. On the mixed corpus, the same pht config (~152 us) beats gperf default (~188 us) [~1.24x, derived from page data], and beats gperf's best mixed config, --inline-strings (~184 us) [~1.21x, derived from page data]. With --string-compare=memcmp, gperf beats every one of the author's hash variants on all three corpora. The keywords-only corpus has no numbers: gperf beats all memcmp variants, and icrc32 with check1memcmp is only 'competitive' with gperf, so pht does NOT win that workload. frozen::unordered_map with lehmer128 is ~85 us (nonkeywords) and ~209 us (mixed), slower than the icrc32/check1memcmp pht in both [derived from page data].

tradeoffs: Perfect-hash tables require the full keyword/key set to be known at build time (code-generation step via generate-pht.cpp / generate-mygperf.py / gperf itself), so they are not usable as a general-purpose associative container; no insertion/deletion at runtime; many generated variants trade code size and branch-predictability for speed (e.g. AES-hasher variants generate much larger .cpp files than FNV/lehmer128 ones); results are highly sensitive to table-size, hasher choice (icrc32/fnv1a32/lehmer128/pearson8/aes/xx364), string-compare strategy (memcmp/check1memcmp/chunk84/cmpestri/sse2/ptest), and CPU features (msse4/maes/cmov), meaning the 'winning' configuration is workload- and hardware-specific rather than a single drop-in replacement.

The table has 7 host/arch columns on 5 hosts: jak-x230 and backup (amd64), asachi.d.o (arm64/armel/armhf), plummer.d.o (ppc64el), and eller.d.o (mipsel). Other competitors are re2c, djb hash variants, and APT's AlphaHash.

On jak-x230 (amd64, Core i5-3320M), Trie is 2.4 vs gperf 1.3 case-sensitive [~1.85x, derived from page data], and Trie (*) is 2.2 vs gperf (*) 0.7 case-insensitive [~3.1x, derived from page data]. tradeoffs: Order-preserving (unlike most minimal perfect hash schemes), which trades some construction flexibility for keeping key order in the output table. Generator only handles a fixed key set known at generation time (codegen tool, like gperf, not a runtime container).
caveats: The benchmark code is not in the triehash repo. It lives in github.com/julian-klode/hashbench (MIT, 0 stars, last commit 2016-10-06), which the author's 2016-09-25 blog post links.
